text:
A U.N. General Assembly committee has passed a resolution on North Korea's human rights situation for the 22nd straight year, expressing concerns over Pyongyang's digital surveillance and technology-enabled repression of its people and other abuses, Seoul's foreign ministry said Thursday.
The Third Committee, which handles human rights and social affairs, adopted the resolution with 95 votes in favor, 14 against and 58 abstentions at the U.N. headquarters in New York on Wednesday (local time), sending it to the General Assembly for final approval in December.
The United States abstained for the first time, taking issue with a reference in the text to the International Criminal Court (ICC), which Washington has accused of exceeding its jurisdiction and infringing on national sovereignty.
Like previous versions, this year's resolution condemned and expressed concerns over the "systematic, widespread and gross" violations of human rights in North Korea "that may amount to crimes against humanity," and the failure to bring those responsible to justice.
It also noted concerns that the overall situation in the North has not improved over the last dozen years, and has, in many instances, degraded.
The resolution raised fresh concerns over issues of the North's digital surveillance and technology-enabled repression as it highlighted the need to address state restrictions on the rights to liberty of movement, as well as freedom of thought, conscience, religion and belief.
At South Korea's proposal, the resolution included language stressing the importance of dialogue and engagement with North Korea, including inter-Korean talks, while calling for progress on humanitarian issues, including families separated by the 1950-53 Korean War and those abducted by North Korea, according to the ministry.
Before the vote on the resolution, North Korean Ambassador to the U.N. Kim Song denounced the annual submission of the resolution as a "politically motivated provocation" aimed at tarnishing North Korea's image and undermining its ideology and political system.
U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Economic and Social Council Dan Negrea said that the U.S. could not support the resolution as drafted because of the language on the ICC, stressing that its abstention is "not a reflection on the situation" in the North.
The U.S.' abstention came as U.S. President Donald Trump has expressed his desire to reengage with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un amid speculation that their talks could materialize during his ongoing trip to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week.
"The U.S. had long championed respect for human rights in the DPRK, including at the U.N.," Negrea said. DPRK stands for North Korea's official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea. "We have supported this resolution since 2004, and we have co-sponsored it in every U.N. General Assembly session for the past 22 years."
He added that the U.S. commitment to promoting human rights, accountability and access to independent information for North Koreans is "unwavering."
Those that supported the resolution at the committee session included South Korea, Britain, France and Canada, while countries with close ties to North Korea, such as China, Russia, Cuba and Iran, voted against it.
The Third Committee has adopted the resolution annually since 2005 to shine a light on human rights violations in the North and redouble international calls for Pyongyang to tackle the issue.
